title: Advanced Redirections: fds & exec 📂
description: Take full control of file descriptors. Redirect entire scripts, clone streams, and close descriptors safely.

slides.title: File Descriptors Refresher 🧾
slides.content:
## The Numbers Behind Streams

- `0` – stdin
- `1` – stdout
- `2` – stderr
- `3‑9` – available for custom use

You've used `>` (default stdout) and `2>` for stderr. Now we'll go deeper.

slides.title: Redirecting Input with <
slides.content: Instead of `cat file`, use `< file` to feed a file's content to a command's stdin:

quizData.question: Which file descriptor number represents stderr?
quizData.explanation: 0 is stdin, 1 is stdout, 2 is stderr.

slides.title: Duplicating Descriptors 🪞
slides.content:
## `m>&n` and `m<&n`

You can make one descriptor point to another:
- `2>&1` – redirect stderr to wherever stdout currently goes.
- `1>&2` – redirect stdout to stderr.
- `&>file` – shortcut to send both stdout and stderr to `file`.

Order matters: `>file 2>&1` writes stdout to file, then merges stderr into that.

slides.title: Complex Redirects
slides.content: Write both stdout and stderr to separate files:

quizData.question: `command 2>&1 >file` redirects stderr to the same file as stdout.
quizData.explanation: It redirects stderr to the original stdout (terminal), then stdout to file. The order is wrong; use `>file 2>&1`.

slides.title: The `exec` Command for Permanent Redirects 🔒
slides.content:
## Redirect the Script Itself

`exec` without a command can alter the file descriptors of the current shell.
- `exec >logfile` – redirects stdout of the entire script from that point on.
- `exec 2>errfile` – stderr to a file.
- `exec 0<file` – read stdin from a file.
- `exec 3>file` – open a custom descriptor for writing.

To restore, save the original descriptor first: `exec 3>&1` (backup stdout), then later `exec 1>&3 3>&-` (restore and close).

slides.title: exec in Action
slides.content: Save all output to a log:
slides.codeSnippet:
exec >script.log 2>&1
echo "This goes to the log"
date

slides.title: Closing Descriptors and /dev/fd 🗑️
slides.content:
## `m>&-` or `m<&-`

Close a file descriptor:
- `exec 3>&-` closes writing descriptor 3.

Special path `/dev/fd/N` represents the file descriptor N as a file. Example: `diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2)` uses `/dev/fd/` under the hood.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `exec` to set up logging at the start of a script. It ensures every `echo` is captured without sprinkling `>>` everywhere.
